title: Fix Unsafe Secret File Permissions
overview:
# Introduction

You are reviewing a small Linux application after a support session where operators loosened file permissions to keep the service moving. The application still needs its API token to work, but the current mode now exposes that secret to users who should not be able to read it.

Before the host review is closed, you need to confirm the permission problem, tighten the secret file back to a safer boundary, and make sure the service still reads it successfully. This is a common least-privilege correction on Linux systems.

The important boundary is local file readability: the service path needs the token, but unrelated local users should not be able to read it.

sections.title: Tighten the Secret File Permissions
sections.content:
# Tighten the Secret File Permissions

You are reviewing a small service that reads a local token file during startup. The service still needs that token, but the file was left readable by every local user, which turns a service credential into host-wide exposure.

This is a permission boundary fix. Inspect the file ownership and mode, remove access for unrelated users, and then prove the application can still read the token through its normal service path.

Avoid over-tightening the file in a way that breaks the service account. The right result narrows access while keeping the intended group-based read path working.

## Current Situation

The project lives at `/home/labex/project`.

The application uses `service-token.txt`, and the `secretapp` service user must keep the access it needs. A project restart helper is provided so you can test the application after changing permissions.

## Scope

Focus on port `18480`, `service-token.txt`, and the service user boundary for this project.

Do not modify the default `labex` user or its sudo access.

## Your Goal

- Move to `/home/labex/project`.
- Inspect `service-token.txt` ownership and permission bits.
- Adjust the mode so the service user and owning group retain read access while others do not.
- Run the application restart helper after permission changes.
- Confirm the application endpoint at `http://127.0.0.1:18480/` still reports success.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `service-token.txt` is no longer world-readable.
- The `secretapp` service path can still read the token successfully.
- The application endpoint at `http://127.0.0.1:18480/` still reports success after restart.
- The default `labex` user and its sudo access remain unchanged.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>What should I inspect first?</summary>

Run `ls -l service-token.txt` from the project directory and note owner, group, and the three digit mode.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What mode matches the requirements?</summary>

The file is `labex:secretapp`. After your change it should still be readable by owner and group but not by others. Apply that with `chmod`, then `./restart-app.sh`, then `curl` port `18480` again.

</details>

sections.title: Summary
sections.content:
# Summary

In this challenge, you corrected a realistic post-support permission drift on a Linux host. You tightened the secret file, removed unnecessary read access, and verified that the application still worked. This reflects a common hardening task: restore least privilege on sensitive files without breaking the service that depends on them.

The secret remains available to the service boundary that needs it, while unrelated local users lose read access.
